catalog_quote: Lexical stress in Ngardi is non - contrastive . Stress assignment in Ngardi is predictable from the syllabic and morphological structure of a phonological word . In nearly all cases, a primary stress is located at the left edge of a word . ... left edge of the word and secondary stresses are subsequently assigned on the heads of all remaining feet . ... Ngardi shows some evidence for weight sensitivity in the assignment of secondary stresses . Light syllables are open syllables with a short vowel while heavy syllables are syllables with codas and / or long vowels . Heavy syllables permit secondary stresses in subsequent adjacent syllables should they form their own well - formed ... do not attract primary stress away from initial position, as shown in ( 72) . ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the survey classification: primary stress on the word-initial syllable, secondary stresses on alternating syllables thereafter; no codes for exceptions (E), quantity-sensitivity (quantity-sensitive) or morphological conditioning (M) are attached to the Ngardi entry.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Category I = 'secondary stress on alternates' (rhythmic alternation from the initial main stress); whether final syllables may bear secondary stress is explicitly left unindicated.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Ngardi; the appendix preface cautions that some entries rest on scanty material and 'may be that some of them have been mistakenly placed in a certain category'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress-type classification in a typological survey appendix; second-hand, citing Menning & Nash (1981) Sourcebook. The modern primary description (Ennever 2021 §2.6 'lexical stress', within ch. 2 pp. 44-105) exists but could not be opened; its p.44 confirms the section exists and calls the prosodic description 'preliminary'.
new_statements.identity_note: Goedemans 1998 lists the language as 'Ngardi (T93)' using Tindale numbering and cites Menning & Nash's Central Australian sourcebook; this is most plausibly the Balgo/Tanami Ngardi = ngar1288 (Ngumpin-Yapa), the same variety as Cataldi 2011, Honeyman 2005 and Ennever 2021 (speakers at Balgo, Ringer Soak, Malan, Kurrurungku, Lajamanu), but the Tindale-number identity was not independently verified. Note older literature sometimes confused 'Ngardi/Ngarti' labels in this region (O'Grady et al.'s 'Ngarga'/Yapa classification vs McConvell's Ngumpin reclassification, per Browne 2024 held by the project).
